name: Setipiprant

lead: Setipiprant is an experimental oral drug that blocks the PGD2 receptor CRTH2 (DP2). Hair-loss communities follow it as a way to protect follicles from shrinking and keep thickness and hairline in male pattern hair loss.

It was developed by Actelion for asthma and seasonal allergies, then taken up for hair loss after a 2012 finding that PGD2 is elevated in balding scalp. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial in men finished in 2018 without a statistically significant improvement over placebo.

paras: It was used only within clinical trials as an oral drug. It has not been marketed for any use.
Early trials reported no severe adverse effects distinguishable from placebo. It is unapproved and not marketed.

angle.text: Setipiprant is followed in hair-loss circles as an investigational drug that blocks prostaglandin D2 signalling, which is elevated in balding scalp, to keep follicles from miniaturising. It began as an allergy and asthma drug. In its phase 2a hair trial it did not beat placebo.

lead: Setipiprant (ACT-129968, later KYTH-105) is an investigational oral drug that selectively blocks the DP2 (CRTH2) receptor for prostaglandin D2.[1][2] It was developed by Actelion for asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, then taken up for androgenetic alopecia after a 2012 finding that PGD2 is elevated in balding scalp.[1]

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial in men with androgenetic alopecia finished in 2018 without a statistically significant improvement over placebo, according to Wikipedia.[1][3] The drug is not approved for any use.

paras: Setipiprant was identified as a potent, selective, orally bioavailable CRTH2 antagonist in a 2013 medicinal chemistry paper from the Actelion programme.[4]

PGD2 acts through DP1, CRTH2 (DP2) and TP receptors; CRTH2 mediates migration and activation of Th2 lymphocytes, eosinophils and basophils.[5] Human studies describe its tolerability, pharmacokinetics, metabolism and formulation bioavailability.[6][7]

Actelion developed setipiprant for allergic disease; development for asthma stopped as it offered no clear advantage over existing drugs.[1] Kythera acquired it for hair loss, and Allergan later acquired Kythera.[1]

In allergic asthmatics, setipiprant reduced allergen-induced airway responses in a double-blind crossover study.[8] Phase 2 and 3 seasonal allergic rhinitis studies reported efficacy and safety results.[9] Registered trials include a phase 2 asthma study (n=438) and a phase 3 rhinitis study (n=630).[10][11]

A phase 2 trial (NCT02781311, n=169) tested setipiprant tablets in men with androgenetic alopecia; the published report describes a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a design.[3][12] Wikipedia reports that the trial did not show a statistically significant improvement over placebo.[1]
Setipiprant is discussed in hair-loss communities as a failed but notable PGD2-pathway candidate. It is not marketed.

timeline.event: PGD2 receptors reported elevated in balding scalp; Kythera acquires setipiprant.[1]
Phase 2a trial concludes without significant benefit.[1]
